question: Which of the following best describes the predominant inflammatory pattern in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), distinguishing it from bronchial asthma?

answers.text: Eosinophilic infiltration with IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and reversible airway obstruction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes bronchial asthma, not COPD. Asthma is characterised by eosinophilic inflammation, IgE-mediated mast cell activation, and reversible bronchoconstriction — which is why inhaled corticosteroids (targeting eosinophilic inflammation) are the cornerstone controller therapy in asthma.

answers.text: Neutrophilic and macrophage-driven inflammation with protease–antiprotease imbalance and irreversible airway obstruction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. COPD is driven by neutrophils and macrophages that release proteases (especially neutrophil elastase), overwhelming antiprotease defences (α1-antitrypsin). This causes alveolar wall destruction (emphysema) and irreversible airway obstruction — explaining why bronchodilators, not anti-inflammatory agents, are the primary maintenance therapy.

answers.text: Histamine-mediated mucosal oedema confined to the nasal epithelium with nasal polyp formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern is characteristic of allergic rhinitis and nasal polyposis, not COPD. While rhinitis shares the 'united airway' with lower airway diseases, its inflammatory mediator profile (predominantly histamine) and mucosal localisation are distinct from COPD.

answers.text: CD4+ T-lymphocyte infiltration with non-caseating granuloma formation in the airway wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes pulmonary sarcoidosis, a granulomatous disease, not COPD. COPD involves CD8+ T-lymphocytes (not CD4+) alongside neutrophils and macrophages, and does not produce granulomata.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pathophysiology section again. The key distinction: asthma = eosinophilic + reversible; COPD = neutrophilic/macrophage + irreversible. This determines why ICS is first-line in asthma but bronchodilators are first-line in COPD.

Excellent. Recognising that COPD is neutrophilic/macrophage-driven with irreversible obstruction — while asthma is eosinophilic with reversible obstruction — is the foundation for understanding why their pharmacotherapy diverges so markedly.
